segments.text: Good morning. You're all ready to go? Excellent. Well, welcome to Against Genomic Discrimination
Aotearoa Agenda. We have Faye Soebi and Professor Andrew Shelling with us today. I'm Sam Affendow,
Chair of the Health Committee. You'll see Government members on my right, Opposition members
not yet here. We have you here for 10 minutes. You may leave us time for questions if you so wish.

Thank you, Chair and members for this opportunity. We ask the Committee to recommend that consultation under sections 83 to 85 of the Contracts of Insurance Act 24 begin before the end of 2026 because delay is a significant public health issue.
New Zealand and Colombia and I learned last night also Costa Rica are at the extreme end of the OECD without operative protection governing insurers use of predictive genetic test results.
The other 35 OECD countries have adopted protections through legislation, regulation, moratoria and industry codes. About one in three New Zealand adults has some form of life insurance

and one in four has private health insurance. Tens of thousands of those insured are likely to carry a re-genetic disorder or an inherited predisposition which is actionable. There is a significant and growing issue at the intersection of genetic testing and insurance.
Genetic testing increasingly diagnoses rare disorders, guides cancer treatment, identifies inherited risk and enables...
all this preventative action before disease develops.
Yet insurers can still request and adversely use the result
affecting the price of availability of cover.
A result can reveal risks across a family,
enabling surveillance, prevention,
shorter diagnostic journeys through cascade testing.
For Māori, genetic information can reach across whakapapa,
making trust and equitable action,
especially important.
If insurance fares to testing,
those opportunities may be lost.
This is not theoretical.
A NZ woman with a BRCA2 variant reports paying premium
subject to a 50% loading for 15 years
despite risk-reducing surgery.
Her daughter was quoted as 75% loading
despite testing negative for the familial variant.
The cases reveal are one-way ratchant.
Adverse results can increase premiums or restrict cover
while negative results and risk-reducing interventions
may receive little favourable weight.
The perverse incentive is the opposite of what we want
for families and what the health system seeks.
Kia ora everyone.
We wish to make a critical distinction
between a predictive genetic test
and the existing diagnosed illness.
We're not proposing any change
to the disclosure of diagnosed illnesses,
symptoms or treatments,
which should remain subject to ordinary underwriting.
What we're looking for is our concern
that an adverse use of a predictive result
in someone who may never develop the condition
may reduce their risks through surveillance,
medication, lifestyle or preventative intervention.
The applicant should remain free
to volunteer favourable results
to improve an insurance outcome.
Evidence in New Zealand and overseas indicates
that those that have concerns about insurance
may deter from un...
genetic testing, and figures show between 10% and 30% will not undertake a genetic test if they've got concerns.
That undermines prevention, early diagnosis, family testing, genomic research and clinical trial recruitment.
One woman we've had contact with learnt that she had a pathogenic variant associated with a cancer syndrome called Lynch syndrome
that enabled her to undertake regular surveillance and risk-reducing surgery.
She was never diagnosed with a Lynch-associated cancer.
Over 10 years, health and life insurance have requested test results and imposed loadings of 50% to 150%.
Imposed exclusions, deferred cover and reduced benefits penalising for knowing and taking action over her genetic result.
We know that screening for inherited conditions can save tens of thousands of lives in New Zealand.
We believe a sustainable insurance market matters, using potentially life-saving information against the person who is in conflict with good health behaviour.
The current system can create an incentive not to test, discourage prevention and shift costs to families in the public health system.
Deterring testing imposes health and economic costs, it does not merely redistribute risk.
Comparable countries show that proportionate protections can coexist with ordinary underwriting.
The UK has predicted genetic results since 2001 in Canada legislated in 2017.
Australia has prevented genetic results being used adversely in health insurance since 2007.
And from the 8th of October this year, Australia will prohibit their adverse use in life insurance underwriting.
It's relevant because our insurance markets are substantially integrated, particularly through life re-insurance.
Despite years of engagement, there's a real risk that effective protection will not be in place when the Act comes into full effect on 15 November 2017.
public health consequences continue to be unaddressed. Section 83-85 provide a regulatory pathway.
We understand that consultation documents are prepared,
but consultation to determine the appropriate New Zealand framework has not begun.
We ask the committee to recognise this as a public health and consumer protection issue
and to recommend to the government that consultation commence before the end of 2026 or sooner.
Recommending consultation would not mean agreement on the final regulatory model.
Consultation is the proper place for all key stakeholders to test the evidence
and design the proportionate safeguards. A genetic test should help us to protect our health
and those we love not penalise us when we apply for insurance. We hope we've got time for questions.
